text:
Accor, Hilton and IHG launched AI discovery tools in 2026.

Booking commissions typically range from 15–30 percent.

Third-party platforms drove most independent hotel bookings in 2025.

ACCOR'S ALL CONCIERGE is the latest example of how hotel owners, franchisees and corporate leadership are using artificial intelligence to put more focus on how guests find and book stays. The way AI mediates that discovery is becoming a distribution-strategy question, alongside OTA commissions, brand-technology fees and guest-acquisition spend.

Accor’s new AI-powered conversational tool, which the company moved from pilot to full-scale rollout this month, guides guests from initial travel inspiration through booking and post-stay support, according to Accor. Hilton and IHG also introduced comparable tools of their own this year, positioning conversational AI as a competitive front across the industry rather than a single company's experiment.

Accor's conversational approach

Accor advances AI with ALL Concierge, a conversational travel companion deployed at scale.Photo credit: Accor

ALL Concierge processed more than 1 million guest conversations since its pilot began in July 2025, insights the company said it used to refine the platform ahead of this wider launch. The tool is available across ALL.com, the ALL Accor app, WhatsApp and iMessage, supporting 11 languages on the website and four languages across five points of sale on mobile, with broader coverage planned by year-end.

“Every great concierge remembers your name and anticipates what you need before you ask,” said Alix Boulnois, Accor's chief commercial, digital and tech officer. “For decades, that level of attention was the privilege of a few. Today, we are making it available to every guest, everywhere, at any hour. And yet, behind every exceptional stay, there will always be a person who cares.”

Our teams are the heart of Accor. What changes today is that they will have a companion just as tireless and attentive, freeing them to focus on what no technology will ever replicate: the human connection that makes hospitality truly memorable.”

Accor has not disclosed adoption figures for the wider rollout. Whether the tool measurably shifts booking behavior away from third-party platforms will depend on guest uptake over time, according to the phased rollout timeline Accor outlined in its announcement.

Boulnois said that Accor's hotel teams remain central to the guest experience even as the tool takes on more of the conversation, adding that support staff can step in whenever a request needs a human touch.

Hilton and IHG are moving in parallel

In March, Hilton launched its AI Planner for curated travel discovery.Photo credit: Hilton Worldwide Holdings

Hilton introduced its own generative AI-powered digital concierge, the Hilton AI Planner, in March, initially in beta to a limited share of hilton.com traffic before expanding, according to Hilton's press release announcing the tool. The tool helps travelers identify destinations, compare properties and explore amenities through conversational search, per the release.

"The launch of the Hilton AI Planner marks another step forward in our journey to reimagine the travel experience for Hilton guests," said Michael Leidinger, Hilton's senior vice president and chief information officer.

IHG Hotels & Resorts launched a beta version of AI-powered conversational search on IHG.com and the IHG One Rewards app in July, the company said. The tool is designed in part to help hotel owners increase their properties' visibility in AI-driven searches, and that it plans to roll out an AI-optimized hotel content platform over the coming months to help owners' properties surface more effectively.

"With these capabilities in place, and more to follow, we are very well positioned to harness the power of AI at scale and deliver rich, inspiring and seamless travel experiences that delight our guests and deliver benefits to our hotel owners," said Elie Maalouf, IHG's chief executive officer, according to the company's release.

Accor also introduced The Butler, a separate AI tool built for hotel staff that provides guidance and information and connects employees with human experts when needed, according to Accor's announcement.

Why it matters to hotel owners and franchisees

OTAs typically charge hotels 15 percent to 30 percent commissions per booking.Photo credit: Istock

The scope of the shift is larger than any single brand's tool, according to Longwoods International's traveler research. The study found that among U.S. travelers who used AI to plan a trip, 54 percent used it to find attractions and activities, 44 percent for travel inspiration and 42 percent for dining options — the same early-journey stages that OTAs and general search engines have historically captured before a guest reaches a hotel brand's own channels, per the study.

Online travel agencies have charged hotel owners commissions typically ranging from 15 percent to 30 percent per booking, depending on the platform, region and partner tier, according to rate disclosures across major OTAs. A 2026 industry report tracking approximately 90 million bookings found that OTAs sourced about 63 percent of independent hotel reservations in 2025, with the share reaching closer to 80 percent in some markets, according to Cloudbeds' State of Independent Hotels report.

For owners and franchisees, that puts AI-native discovery closer to the center of distribution economics rather than at the periphery. A brand's ability to capture guests earlier in the journey — and retain the resulting guest data — can affect guest-acquisition costs and loyalty-program value over time, though the effect will vary by brand, market and how quickly travelers shift habits away from established OTA use.

That raises practical questions for owners and multi-brand operators evaluating brand agreements: how these tools are funded within brand-technology fees, whether participation is mandatory or optional across a portfolio, and what data or reporting owners will receive on whether the tools are actually reducing OTA dependency rather than simply adding a new guest-facing feature.

IHG said its intent to help owners' properties surface more prominently in AI search results, but neither Accor, Hilton nor IHG has yet published data quantifying a shift in booking share away from third-party platforms.

That does not mean AI concierges automatically lower distribution costs. All three tools remain in partial or phased rollout, according to each company's own announcement, and the broader shift toward AI-mediated trip planning could just as easily create a new dependency — on AI platforms rather than OTAs — if hotel brands need visibility inside third-party AI tools to be discovered at all.

name: Ecolab
title: From ambition to action: Operationalizing water circularity as a strategic growth asset
description:
The historical model of industrial water management - built on a linear "Take-Use-Discharge" framework - is rapidly colliding with physical and economic limits.
Because reliable water access underpins approximately 60% of global GDP, industrial operators must undergo a fundamental paradigm shift: treating water infrastructure as a core, strategic growth asset that directly impacts operational throughput, product quality, and long-term business resilience.
To successfully move from ambition to action, forward-thinking operators are abandoning fragmented, isolated water treatments in favor of an integrated, closed-loop approach.
Standardizing excellence: Shifting the benchmarking paradigm The first major hurdle in transitioning to a circular water model is internal perception.
When a facility can quantify its water efficiency gap relative to best-in-class operators, water circularity transforms from a vague environmental aspiration into a clear, justifiable engineering project.
text:
Corporate sustainability has reached an inflection point. Globally, industrial enterprises have spent the past several years announcing ambitious commitments to achieve net-zero carbon emissions, water neutrality, and watershed resilience. Yet, as operations managers and water professionals know all too well, there remains a significant gap between high-level executive commitments and actual execution.

The historical model of industrial water management - built on a linear "Take-Use-Discharge" framework - is rapidly colliding with physical and economic limits. With a projected 56% global freshwater shortfall looming by 2030, water can no longer be viewed as a cheap, infinite commodity or a static utility cost.

Because reliable water access underpins approximately 60% of global GDP, industrial operators must undergo a fundamental paradigm shift: treating water infrastructure as a core, strategic growth asset that directly impacts operational throughput, product quality, and long-term business resilience.

To successfully move from ambition to action, forward-thinking operators are abandoning fragmented, isolated water treatments in favor of an integrated, closed-loop approach. This transition requires a dual-focus playbook: standardizing performance through rigorous benchmarking and engineering outcome-driven operations to drive economic results.

Standardizing excellence: Shifting the benchmarking paradigm

The first major hurdle in transitioning to a circular water model is internal perception. Traditionally, wastewater treatment and effluent compliance have been managed as risk-mitigation cost centers. To reframe water as a strategic asset, organizations must establish a baseline of operational transparency that connects facility data directly to enterprise value.

This is where standardizing excellence through verified benchmarking becomes indispensable. By leveraging established disclosure frameworks and implementing performance metrics like Ecolab and CDP’s Water Use Efficiency Index, industrial operators can objectively evaluate their water performance against global industry peers.

Rather than viewing these indices as simple compliance exercises, advanced facilities utilize them to identify hidden inefficiencies across their unit operations, build a scalable data-backed roadmap, and justify capital deployment for circular water infrastructure. When a facility can quantify its water efficiency gap relative to best-in-class operators, water circularity transforms from a vague environmental aspiration into a clear, justifiable engineering project.

Engineering to outcomes: Navigating interdependencies

Once an organization establishes its baseline, the challenge shifts to physical execution. The primary reason many circular water initiatives stall is a failure to recognize operational interdependencies. An industrial facility is a web of connected thermal and chemical systems; a water treatment decision made at a cooling tower inevitably cascades down to impact heat exchangers, boiler feedwater networks, and wastewater treatment plants.

Taking a purely siloed approach to these units introduces hidden cost drivers and operational risks. True value capture requires an integrated, programmatic systems approach. By conducting comprehensive front-end mapping and a total water-and-energy balance, engineers can design systems that treat distinct wastewater streams independently based on their specific chemical profiles, preparing them for recycling.

This level of circularity helps effluent water to be systematically reclaimed and returned back into operations, maximizing throughput while minimizing raw water intake and discharge fees.

Real-world execution: The circular blueprint in industry

The tangible commercial viability of this programmatic approach is best demonstrated within heavy manufacturing, where extreme water quality and reliable volumes directly dictate product yield.

Consider a steel refining facility in France that produces approximately 700 kilotons of color-coated steel coils for modern architecture annually. To manufacture a premium product, the plant requires an uncompromised supply of high-purity water. Facing an aging pretreatment infrastructure, the facility partnered with Ecolab to execute a comprehensive Total Water Management solution that optimized the site's entire water ecosystem.

The engineering solution integrated a centralized, automated demineralization plant -deployed in four modular, containerized units - with real-time 3D TRASAR™ monitoring and advanced analytics. Concurrently, the facility's existing effluent recycling unit was upgraded, and a specialized chemical dosing platform was introduced to maximize site-wide chemical safety.

By systematically managing the plant's water interdependencies, the facility successfully operationalized its sustainability goals into distinct commercial milestones. The state-of-the-art system consistently maintains the required 70 cubic meters of demineralized water per hour production rate, ensuring maximum manufacturing throughput.

Simultaneously, the upgraded recycling system cut the facility's raw water expenditure by $80,000 per year and eliminated $180,000 of acrylate waste discharge annually. Combined with optimized operational efficiencies and enhanced on-site chemical safety, this programmatic circular design delivers $500,000 in total financial savings to the enterprise every year.

Conclusion: Securing the license to operate

The lessons learned from this example are clear: water circularity is not an operational liability or an expensive compliance burden. When engineered through a programmatic framework that links advanced chemistry, automation, and real-time digital intelligence, water circularity becomes a powerful engine for cost control and productivity.

As local regulations intensify and global freshwater scarcity escalates, the industries that survive and thrive will be those that move past high-level discussion. By implementing a rigorous, data-driven blueprint that treats wastewater as a premium asset rather than a disposable byproduct, forward-thinking operators are successfully securing their future license to operate - decoupling their industrial growth from resource consumption while delivering profound value to the enterprise and the surrounding community alike.

text:
After racking up a trio of regulatory wins overseas, Eli Lilly’s once-weekly insulin is coming home to open a new front in the company’s ongoing market showdown with Novo.

The FDA has signed off on Lilly’s Onswik, also known as insulin efsitora alfa-gobe, as a new once-weekly basal insulin to help keep blood sugar in check in patients with type 2 diabetes.

With the green light, Lilly will now be able to introduce a direct competitor to Novo’s Awiqli in the U.S.

Approved in late March, Awiqli, Novo’s own solution to daily basal insulin shots, has managed to eke out a commercial head start over Lilly’s drug, in a dynamic that echoes the rollout of the companies’ oral obesity medications earlier this year.

Meanwhile, the new FDA go-ahead marks Onswik’s fourth global regulatory win, following actions from regulators in the European Union, Mexico and Japan.

The FDA’s decision leveraged data from Lilly’s late-stage Qwint program, which looked at Onswik in more than 3,400 patients with type 2 diabetes. In each trial, the drug met the primary endpoint of noninferior A1C reduction from baseline compared with insulin glargine or insulin degludec.

Breaking things down, Onswik helped curb patients’ A1C by 1.31% versus 1.27% for insulin glargine at 52 weeks in Qwint-1, which looked at patients with type 2 diabetes using insulin for the first time. The drug reduced A1C by 0.86% at week 26 in Qwint-3 and 1.07% over that same span in Qwint-4, compared with 0.75% for insulin degludec and 1.07% for insulin glargine, respectively.

Qwint-3 assessed patients who had previously used basal insulin, while the fourth Qwint study looked at those who had previously used daily basal insulin and mealtime insulin. Qwint-2, meanwhile, stratified insulin-naive patients based on whether they were also using a GLP-1 receptor agonist. Onswik was noninferior to insulin degludec regardless of GLP-1 use.

By 2030, more than 510 million people around the world are expected to be living with diabetes, mainly in the form of type 2 disease, and some 37 million are expected to use insulin, according to Lilly.

"For over a century, Lilly has been developing insulins that transformed diabetes care for millions of people worldwide, but delays in initiating treatment and the burden of daily injections can have a real impact on patients' day-to-day experience managing type 2 diabetes," said Kenneth Custer, Ph.D., Lilly’s EVP and president of cardiometabolic health, in a statement.

With an approval in hand, Lilly says it plans to launch Onswik in the U.S. “in the coming months.” The company is rolling out the product in 500 units/mL and 1,000 units/mL concentrations.

As Lilly gets its ducks in a row for the Onswik launch, Novo is now coming up on the second month of Awiqli’s U.S. market run. The Danish drugmaker debuted its weekly insulin on Aug. 11.

While insulin remains a key backbone of both Lilly’s and Novo’s businesses, and a reminder of the metabolic medicine makers’ long histories addressing diabetes, the companies’ GLP-1 medicines have stolen center stage in recent years, particularly in their blockbuster obesity indications.

title: Microsoft unveils Copilot super app, targeting business users with AI agents | Fortune
description:
The super app is a major redesign of Microsoft’s existing Copilot app, bringing together a variety of features and capabilities intended to create a Swiss Army knife for AI productivity.
Though there is a free version of the super app, customers will need their Microsoft subscriptions or workplace licenses to unlock its full range of offerings.

Microsoft’s super app reveal also follows a stretch of growing pains for Copilot.
text:
Microsoft is launching its super app as a central interface through which customers can chat with AI bots, tap AI tools to help accomplish tasks, write code, and access a new “Autopilot” feature that brings agentic capabilities — AI that can act on tasks on its own — to the company’s flagship AI app. The super app is a major redesign of Microsoft’s existing Copilot app, bringing together a variety of features and capabilities intended to create a Swiss Army knife for AI productivity. The launch follows a push by Microsoft to merge what had become a sprawling collection of Copilot products that critics said left customers confused.

For Chief Executive Satya Nadella, the new Copilot is a way to win subscriptions in a business that’s become increasingly important to the software maker, while also ensuring that Microsoft’s lucrative productivity offerings don’t get sidelined by a new generation of AI rivals.

The super app, first reported by Fortune in May, also plugs into Microsoft’s Office tools, letting users ask a bot to handle a task on an Excel spreadsheet or change a layout in a Word document. Though there is a free version of the super app, customers will need their Microsoft subscriptions or workplace licenses to unlock its full range of offerings. Both enterprise customers and individual users will have to pay extra based on usage of its most autonomous capabilities.

“We do want this to become an all-in-one productivity suite,” Annie Pearl, corporate vice president of Copilot, told Fortune. That includes being a platform “where you can ask questions, you could delegate complex multi-step work, you can build software for internal and external use cases, and you can automate tasks through your kind of digital worker or personal agent.”

The Autopilot feature lets users name their agent, assign it a role and a goal, then set it loose on tasks such as project updates, tracking work decisions and deadlines, reminding colleagues when commitments are due, gathering prep materials, and reaching out to partners.

The coding feature targets non-software engineers who want to build apps, a dashboard, or other tools and platforms, Pearl said, though she added that it will grow more powerful over time.

Most of the app’s new features are rolling out through an early-test program, and Microsoft has not set a timeline for general availability. The coding tool, which shares its underlying tech stack with Microsoft’s GitHub Copilot, will reach Microsoft 365 Premium and Pro subscribers through the test program later this year. Autopilot will undergo a more restricted phase of user testing, and broad rollout will hinge on how testers rate the new tools.

Competitive pressure

Microsoft is betting the super app will supercharge its Copilot brand by using AI directly connected to the business tools that already make it money. As OpenAI and Anthropic push into enterprise offerings, Microsoft is racing to protect its turf and keep pace with customer expectations. It’s also launching the app just as agentic capabilities break into the mainstream. OpenAI unveiled its own super app in July. Meta Platforms has already seen early success with its new Muse app, which targets general consumers, letting them create a personal agent to handle food orders, bank statements, and other tasks.

Microsoft’s super app reveal also follows a stretch of growing pains for Copilot. Nadella has shaken up executive ranks to position the company competitively against the top AI labs and enterprise rivals, forging a unified Copilot team earlier this year that merged the consumer and enterprise sides under Jacob Andreou, the fast-rising executive now in charge of Copilot.

Copilot stumbled early, plagued by branding issues, limited capabilities, and Microsoft’s decision to launch several versions of the AI that confused customers. Its consumer Copilot failed to reach mainstream success. More recently, as Microsoft has refocused on enterprise and streamlined its operations, it’s found some traction. In July, the company said its Microsoft 365 Copilot had surpassed 30 million paid seats, with net seats added doubling quarter over quarter. Its shares have rebounded over the past six months on the strength of its cloud computing business, fueled by AI demand and Copilot growth.

Security concerns

Copilot relies mostly on models from Anthropic and OpenAI, though it also accesses xAI’s Grok models, Pearl said. Security has also been a top concern, especially as models from OpenAI and Anthropic have been used to hack into other companies in recent months, stoking worldwide unease about AI capabilities. On Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent infiltrated an Australian government website in June, marking the latest such incident.

Microsoft said it has built several safety guards into its app. Those include rules requiring its Autopilot agents to carry explicit permissions, full audit logs, and tracking. Humans decide how much autonomy an agent receives, the company said. When non-developers build apps using the Code tool, the software runs tasks in isolated local or cloud-hosted environments, with controls intended to protect customer data and systems.

“Everything that you observe should be governable by policy,” Nadella told customers this week at a presentation at Microsoft’s Redmond, Wash. headquarters. “That’s the classic thing we have done for decades when it comes to IT management, and now I need to do that with every agent out there.

“The way we have conceptualized Copilot is to think of this not as just any one product or one form factor, but as a system that brings form and function together.”

Microsoft also plans to monetize the new features by charging extra for its best capabilities. Seats paid for by enterprise customers or individual users cover “everyday AI” such as Chat, Office integration, and standard routing, while usage-based billing can apply to Code, Autopilot, and access to the newest, most capable AI models.

Microsoft also plans future add-ons that would tie in even more of its ecosystem. That includes a function called “Today,” which Microsoft says will integrate emails, calendar, Teams, and tasks to organize and prioritize workloads. It will actively complete tasks, such as generating drafts, proposing schedule updates, and setting up follow-ups for quick user action, the company said.

title: OpenAI has a Mark Zuckerberg-shaped problem - Business Insider
description:
OpenAI's ChatGPT is still the face of consumer AI.
Meta's Muse agent overtook ChatGPT on the free app charts this week, part of a new craze over personal AI assistants in Silicon Valley.
Meta is adding Muse to its smart glasses and building a new Tamagotchi-esque gadget called Muse Charm, it announced at its Connect conference on Wednesday.
He replied to a post about agents, showing notifications from Muse, Instinct, and Grok Bot and saying "it's enough," with a hand-wave emoji.
Meta's smart glasses have also turned into a hit, giving it another touchpoint for the Muse assistant.
text:
OpenAI's ChatGPT is still the face of consumer AI. But it's no longer the hot new thing.

Meta's Muse agent overtook ChatGPT on the free app charts this week, part of a new craze over personal AI assistants in Silicon Valley. Muse can browse, click, type, and chat across the internet, handling tasks you give it. Meta is adding Muse to its smart glasses and building a new Tamagotchi-esque gadget called Muse Charm, it announced at its Connect conference on Wednesday.

The capabilities aren't new; ChatGPT can do many of the same things. At the same time, Muse's explosive growth is still a major headache for OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

Muse proves that an AI tool can handle work without relying on OpenAI's frontier models. It shows that Meta will pour huge amounts of money into keeping a ChatGPT competitor free. And it signals that OpenAI's longtime push into "browser use" — one of the capabilities that Muse rests on — isn't turning into a moat.

OpenAI hasn't launched a direct answer to Muse, though it could easily do so at its DevDay conference on Tuesday.

As early adopters suss out new AI assistant options, OpenAI risks getting left behind. There's Instinct, from a tiny startup run by a 23-year-old. There's SpaceXAI's Grok Bot and Google's Gemini Spark, with all the firepower of those giant companies. And then there's Muse, bolstered by Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg's aggressive growth tactics.

The internet has begun rumbling about rumors of a competitor from OpenAI. And Thibault Sottiaux, an OpenAI product leader, teased a release. He replied to a post about agents, showing notifications from Muse, Instinct, and Grok Bot and saying "it's enough," with a hand-wave emoji.

"Everyone is sort of circling around this," Techsponential analyst Avi Greengart told Business Insider.

He said each assistant launch fits a general trend from the companies: they're "all trying to arrive at a durable and monetizable way to use AI to, hopefully, improve people's lives."

Meta's apps dominate for consumers

OpenAI's chief rival has always been Anthropic, and all the while, OpenAI owned a major advantage: ChatGPT is way bigger than Claude. OpenAI's tool hit 1 billion weekly active users this year.

Against Meta, that brag won't fly. Zuckerberg's empire extends to more than 3 billion daily active users across Instagram, Facebook, Messenger, and WhatsApp. It's easy for Meta to promote a new tool to vast numbers of users, plus the company's advertising business prints enough cash to fund billions in AI compute. Meta's smart glasses have also turned into a hit, giving it another touchpoint for the Muse assistant.

More than 2.5 million people downloaded Muse on mobile in the 13 days after its launch, according to Sensor Tower, a market intelligence firm.

Seema Shah, vice president of insights at the firm, told Business Insider she sees Muse's simplicity as its biggest draw. The assistant lives in a messenger-style window, handles work quickly, and has garnered rave reviews from techie first adopters. And though it's meant to handle work, it also answers questions, like ChatGPT.

Instinct, similarly, leans into ease of use as a selling point — you don't need to download an app. You just text it.

If the tools continue their boom in popularity, they could eat into OpenAI's attempt to make it a one-stop shop for work.

OpenAI's response could arrive within days

Shah expects OpenAI to launch something similar to Muse and Instinct.

And on Monday, the Information reported that OpenAI is developing features to compete with the new AI assistant apps. We could see the response very soon. Altman wrote on X that he's excited for something big to ship next week, when OpenAI holds its yearly DevDay conference.

Shah said that in this still-early stage of AI competition, she assumes no top company wants to be left out of any popular market. She said that despite Muse's speedy growth, the contest is far from over since retention indicates success better than the early wave of downloads.

"Even within the chatbots, there are different levels of engagement, different levels of churn, different levels of retention," Shah said. "And ChatGPT is the most successful in those metrics at the moment."

text:
Microsoft introduced an updated version of its Copilot app on Friday, combining AI chat, coding tools, and autonomous agents into a single product as the company tries to expand adoption among business customers and counter competition from Anthropic and OpenAI.

The new app is organized around three sections. Home brings together conversational chat and a task-delegation feature called Cowork, and also embeds full versions of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint so users can create and edit documents without leaving Copilot. Code allows non-technical users to build apps, dashboards, and automations by describing them in plain language, using the same underlying technology as GitHub Copilot. Autopilot, previously called Scout, lets users create always-on agents that run in the cloud, monitor email and Teams channels, and carry out recurring tasks without waiting for a new prompt, the company said.

Microsoft has sold its 365 Copilot AI assistant and its GitHub Copilot coding agent as separate products. The new app combines those functions in a single experience. Fewer than 7% of more than 450 million commercial Microsoft 365 seats carry Copilot licenses, according to CNBC. Microsoft reported more than 30 million paid Copilot seats in July.

The launch also comes with a pricing shift. A monthly per-user license keeps covering standard functions — chat and the Copilot capabilities built into Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams — while Cowork, Code, and Autopilot will be metered by consumption, as will the newest frontier models, the company said. Microsoft Chief Executive Officer Satya Nadella told investors in July that the company is moving "beyond per-seat to per-seat-plus-consumption," according to GeekWire.

Jacob Andreou, Microsoft's executive vice president for Copilot, told CNBC that the company is "holding a very high bar" and that the product performs best when it focuses on delivering value and quality to users. He acknowledged that adding coding to the app represents an instance of Microsoft playing catch-up, according to CNBC.

Copilot continues to draw on models from OpenAI and Anthropic alongside Microsoft's own. Within the coding product, users can choose from several models, including one from Microsoft, though no Microsoft model appears among the options in the Home tab, according to CNBC.

text:
Scott Wilson knows what it is like to make a contrarian bet that pays off big. His early investment in SpaceX helped create a multi-billion dollar windfall for Washington University's endowment.

Now he's making another one: The trillion-dollar AI labs are in major trouble.

Wilson argues that OpenAI and Anthropic have committed to enormous spending just as cheaper Chinese models are catching up. It's a view that puts him squarely at odds with AI bulls like Vinod Khosla, who believes those massive infrastructure investments are precisely what will make the frontier labs hard to beat.

"These trillion-dollar-plus frontier companies are not worth the liabilities that they signed up for," Wilson said. "There's going to be a ton of free alternatives."

OpenAI has returned huge markups for VC firms as well as schools such as the University of Michigan, whose early $20 million OpenAI investment is now worth over $2 billion. Wilson said he also had the chance to be an early investor in OpenAI but passed because he was not convinced the company would ever make money. Since then, his bearish view has hardened.

"When we looked at the original OpenAI deal that some of our peers participated in and made tons of money on paper, we were highly skeptical," Wilson said. "I've gotten more skeptical over time."

Wilson shared what he called his "unpopular opinion" onstage last week at Rock Yard Roundup, a Fort Worth gathering of roughly 100 asset managers, VCs, and tech founders. Between a honky-tonk crawl and a visit to the Stockyards Rodeo, he cast the frontier AI race as its own kind of Wild West: a frenzy of runaway spending and valuations that, in his view, is unlikely to end well.

Wilson's warning comes as Chinese model makers such as DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen, Zhipu AI, and Tencent have narrowed the gap with U.S. frontier labs on performance while offering major cost savings. That has fueled a broader investor debate over whether OpenAI and Anthropic, which is expected to go public next month, can sustain the enormous spending required to stay ahead if customers can switch to cheaper alternatives that are almost as good.

Wilson explained that he has become more dubious about frontier labs after talking to his colleagues on the ground in China, who have seen rapid progress in open-weight models. He grew more concerned after speaking with the founders of companies Washington University has invested in, who told him they were all switching to cheaper models.

"Whenever we talk to our portfolio companies, especially the ones who are heavy of AI, they are all moving aggressively towards open source," he said. "It's like any other high-cost U.S. good that has to compete with a low-cost import, particularly from China."

Khosla says he's never been more bullish on OpenAI

Data from OpenRouter, a platform where developers route requests among AI models, supports Wilson's argument, though it is a limited snapshot. DeepSeek accounts for 25.3% of text-model requests on OpenRouter compared with 18.6% for OpenAI and 2.9% for Anthropic.

Khosla, a billionaire venture investor who was an early investor in OpenAI, told Business Insider he strongly disagrees with Wilson and said he has never been more bullish on OpenAI.

"People like that are silly, and they don't understand how this works," he said when told of Wilson's view. "They have this notion that the model is the value."

Khosla argued that the real advantage lies in controlling more of the expensive infrastructure beneath the model. A closed-model company can co-design chips, as OpenAI has done with its Jalapeño inference chip, around its own models and serving systems. That could reduce its reliance on Nvidia hardware and third-party cloud services, he said, lowering its cost to serve customers relative to an open-weight model run on someone else's cloud.

"I'm not talking price, I'm talking about cost," he said. "From power to data center to chips, to infrastructure software to inference models, the cost of the stack is almost certainly going to be lower in closed-source models than open-source."

text:
For years, the hotel concierge has been the person guests turn to for everything from finding the right room to arranging a last-minute dinner reservation. Accor is now bringing that familiar role into the digital space with ALL Concierge, a conversational AI companion designed to assist travellers through almost every stage of a hotel journey.

Accor announced the full-scale launch of ALL Concierge on September 24, following a pilot that began in July 2025. The hospitality group says it is the first time a major hotel company has moved beyond testing and deployed a fully conversational AI companion at scale. The service is designed to stay with travellers from the moment they begin looking for a holiday, helping them discover, and compare hotels, through booking and post-stay support.

Rather than functioning as a conventional customer-service chatbot, ALL Concierge is built around an ongoing conversation. Travellers can describe the kind of holiday they have in mind, including their preferred travel style, mood or experience, and receive hotel suggestions accordingly. They can then ask for more information about individual properties, including details such as breakfast timings, restaurant menus, and spa facilities, before moving to Accor's booking platform.

The service also extends beyond the point of booking. Guests can use it to ask questions about existing reservations, access real-time support, and manage aspects of their stay. Returning ALL Accor members can be recognised by the system, allowing responses to draw on information such as their loyalty profile, previous stays, and preferences.

Speed is another part of the proposition. Accor says ALL Concierge can respond in under a few seconds and handle most requests independently. When a query requires human intervention, the conversation can be transferred to a support team member, allowing the digital interaction to continue without starting over.

The rollout is also designed to meet travellers where they already spend time online. ALL Concierge is available through the ALL.com website and the ALL Accor app, as well as WhatsApp, and iMessage. It currently supports 11 languages on ALL.com, with Accor planning to expand language availability further by the end of 2026.

The technology has been shaped by more than one million guest conversations recorded during the pilot phase. According to Accor, the testing showed that travellers were using conversational AI for more than customer service. They turned to it for travel inspiration, destination and hotel discovery, comparisons, and support throughout their journey.

The current version is therefore positioned less as a standalone booking tool and more as a continuous digital layer across the guest experience. On the ALL Accor app, the service is currently available in four languages across five points of sale, with deployment across all points of sale planned by the end of the year.

The Butler is intended to give hotel teams quick access to information, guidance, recommendations and operational support during their working day. It can also connect employees with the appropriate human experts when a situation requires further assistance. The aim is to reduce the time teams spend navigating routine information and leave them with more time for direct guest interactions.

The guest-facing ALL Concierge is also set to gain more capabilities. Planned developments include AI-assisted hotel comparisons using maps and synthesised guest reviews, destination comparisons based on specific criteria, and personalised recommendations for earning and using ALL Accor points.

The service is also expected to recommend local events and activities through partners such as Fever, with ALL members eventually able to use reward points to book selected experiences. Future updates will allow guests to modify or cancel reservations through the conversational interface, retrieve hotel invoices, and track loyalty points after a stay.

Accor is also working towards taking the experience beyond text. A voice-enabled version is planned to connect ALL Concierge with Accor contact centres and hotel phone lines, allowing travellers to receive verbal assistance through the same conversational system.

Together, ALL Concierge and The Butler mark Accor's attempt to use AI across both sides of hospitality: helping travellers navigate their stays while giving hotel teams another digital tool for everyday operations. The broader rollout also signals a shift in how hotel groups are positioning conversational AI, moving it from a customer-service feature towards an always-available travel companion.

text:
Microsoft is shifting its strategy for its Copilot AI platform as the software giant keeps looking for momentum in enterprise AI, where Anthropic has been gaining traction.

On Friday, Microsoft introduced an updated Copilot app that can both code and handle complex productivity tasks, a move the company hopes will entice more of its Office 365 customers to pay for the advanced tools.

While Microsoft maintains a dominant position in business software through Office, its flagship work AI product hasn't taken off. Of more than 450 million existing commercial Office 365 seats across the globe, fewer than 7% have licenses for the AI addition.

Microsoft has, to this point, offered its 365 Copilot AI assistant for knowledge work separately from its GitHub Copilot coding agent. The market has been consolidating around easy-to-use products from OpenAI and Anthropic that bundle various functions. Microsoft's launch comes after CEO Satya Nadella, in June, talked up a future Copilot "super app."

Rather than charging for subscriptions like it does for most of its software — the commercial Microsoft 365 Copilot costs $30 per user per month — Microsoft says clients will pay for the Cowork, Code and Autopilot portions of the new app based on usage, similar to how they buy other AI products.

"We're holding a very high bar," Jacob Andreou, Microsoft's executive vice president for Copilot, told CNBC. "This product is at its best when it's just optimizing for user value and for the quality of the output and what it's able to deliver." Cost efficiency is less important, he said.

Microsoft shares are up 3% this year as of Thursday's close, underperforming the Nasdaq and most of the company's megacap peers.

The new Code feature makes it easy for non-technical users to start simple AI-driven programming projects, and is based on the same technology as GitHub Copilot. An Autopilot tab will allow users to create custom agents that can take care of assignments and communicate in Teams and Outlook.

David McLaren, enterprise data and AI leader at consulting firm GHD, said his company has given Microsoft Copilot to 12,000 employees, with around 200 experimenting with Copilot Cowork, which can handle more complex tasks.

McLaren told CNBC that he's excited for the new app "because it makes GitHub-like capability simpler for more people to use."

Microsoft faces an increasingly crowded AI agent market. Meta's Muse app, introduced earlier this month, has shot up to the top of Apple's App Store, following the rising popularity of tools like Instinct and the open-source OpenClaw.

"The problem is that these agents have been almost impossible to bring into the enterprise," Andreou said at a Wednesday product preview for customers in Seattle. He acknowledged to CNBC that adding the coding element to the app is an instance of Microsoft playing catch-up.

And in catering to user demands, Microsoft is still leaning on the foremost models from OpenAI and Anthropic even as it invests in its own models.

With the new app, users of the coding product can manually select which model they want to use, including a cost-efficient offering from Microsoft. In the Home tab, where users go for productivity requests like generating a report and scheduling changes, there's no Microsoft model available.

Companies enrolled in Microsoft's Frontier program, which provides access to the newest features, will be able to use the Home and Code tabs in the coming weeks, with the Autopilot available in private preview by the end of this month.

"When I think about the Frontier program, this is not about any one frontier model," Nadella said at Wednesday's event. "It's about the frontier ecosystem that we want to ensure, where every firm is able to take their human capital that's in the flow of AI, and then being able to build out this continuous learning system."

text:
Mike Blake | Tom Little | Reuters

Every time Novo urges investors to look ahead, Eli Lilly gives them another reason to look back at its widening lead over the Danish drugmaker.

Novo this week laid out an ambitious strategy to reignite growth beyond its top-selling Wegovy and Ozempic injections, which face patent expirations in key markets in the early 2030s. At its Capital Markets Day on Monday, the company promised a pipeline of potential blockbuster products, including drugs that would diversify from its core area of obesity and diabetes.

But Wall Street so far isn't convinced by Novo's road map. Investors pummeled the drugmaker's stock, underwhelmed by growth targets that matched industry averages rather than outpacing them. They were also skeptical of the lack of clarity around a near-term turnaround plan.

At the same time, Lilly continues to chip away at its rival's market share — including in the burgeoning obesity pill space.

Novo hopes to keep its early lead in the oral weight loss market after the successful launch of the Wegovy pill, months ahead of Lilly's rival pill, Foundayo. Novo CEO Mike Doustdar told CNBC on Tuesday that early adoption suggests patients may have been waiting for an alternative to injections.

"If that continues to the extent that we have seen, then yes, mathematically, by the end of the decade, there is going to be a larger portion on the pill than injectable," he said.

But Lilly is hot on its heels, backed by its commercial firepower.

In an exclusive interview with CNBC on Monday, Lilly CEO Dave Ricks said the drugmaker's new obesity pill, Foundayo, is slowly gaining ground in the U.S. One-third of new GLP-1 pill patients are taking Lilly's drug, and its share of that oral market is growing "week by week," Ricks told CNBC in Houston, Texas.

Lilly is also claiming an early lead in the newly established Medicare market for obesity drugs, after the federal program started covering those treatments in July. Ricks said 700,000 seniors have started GLP-1s in Medicare following the start of coverage, and 70% of those patients are on Lilly's drugs.

He added that Medicare patients have shown a particular preference for Lilly's obesity injection Zepbound, which has helped the company become the dominant player in the broader market. Lilly said in August that it held about a 61% share in the U.S. GLP-1 space in the second quarter, while Novo held roughly 39%.

While investors appeared to want more detail on Novo's plans for post-Wegovy and Ozempic growth at Monday's investor event, the drugmaker is betting that there could be more than one successor to the mega-blockbuster franchise.

For Novo, the challenge is not solely replacing revenue from Wegovy and Ozempic when they lose exclusivity and face more generic competition. It is convincing investors that the company can regain momentum in a GLP-1 market it helped establish years before Lilly came into the picture, even as its rival continues to build its lead.

Lilly likely to keep its upper hand

watch now

Even as Novo works to turn itself around after two bruising years marked by multiple setbacks, analysts say Lilly has several advantages that could help it maintain its spot at the top of the obesity drug market.

"Lilly is in the leadership position, and we think that they will remain in this strong leadership position, given their substantial commercial advantage, their global initiative to globalize their products further, and then their advanced pipeline of novel candidates as well," Leerink Partners analyst David Risinger said in an interview.

Risinger expects Foundayo's share of the oral GLP-1 market to continue growing, pointing to Lilly's "tremendous commercial firepower" and greater spending capacity to promote the drug. But Risinger expects Foundayo to eventually dominate the pill market globally, in part because it should be less costly to manufacture at scale than the Wegovy pill.

Foundayo is a small-molecule drug, which can be manufactured differently and more easily at scale than peptide drugs such as Novo's Wegovy pill and existing injectable GLP-1s. While Foundayo leads to less weight loss on average than the Wegovy pill, it doesn't carry any food and water restrictions, which could be a selling point for some patients.

Novo executives this week did not directly answer questions about whether Foundayo is easier to manufacture and scale. Novo is investing billions in manufacturing facilities and, executives said this week, the company aims to be able to increase the number of patients on its GLP-1 drugs tenfold by 2030. Executives have repeatedly said supply is not an issue and that Novo will not face the same shortages it did with injectable versions in the earlier days of Ozempic and Wegovy.

For Lilly, Zepbound's higher efficacy than the original doses of Wegovy has also been key to securing its market share lead over Novo in the injectable space. Novo has sought to narrow that efficacy gap with a higher-dose version of Wegovy launched this year, which leads to roughly similar weight loss as Zepbound.

But Lilly is not standing still.

The company has a pipeline of next-generation obesity drugs that could extend its lead beyond Zepbound and Foundayo, Risinger said. That includes retatrutide, a triple-agonist that targets three gut hormones and has produced greater weight loss than existing obesity drugs in clinical trials. Lilly plans to seek approval for the drug in the first quarter of 2027.

Lilly is also developing a weekly injection that targets the amylin receptor, a pathway involved in appetite and satiety that differs from those targeted by existing treatments. Risinger said the drug has "much greater potential than the Street currently realizes," particularly because a large population of patients does not tolerate or respond adequately to GLP-1 drugs.

"We're quite enthusiastic about the company's pipeline for follow-on agents beyond Zepbound and Foundayo," Risinger said.

While investors have been laser-focused on the headline weight loss number of Novo and Lilly's next-generation drugs, Novo sees a fragmented market ahead.

Chief Scientific Officer Martin Holst Lange told CNBC this week that the breadth of Novo's future pipeline would give physicians and patients more options and increase uptake. The company is studying the effect of new drugs on factors like tolerability, muscle preservation, their effect on obesity-linked conditions, convenience and more.

"We can't do that with one single drug," Lange said.

Novo bets on its next generation

Andrew Caballero-Reynolds | Afp | Getty Images

For Novo, the answer to Lilly's dominance is a sweeping bet on what comes next.

Novo is targeting the launch of more than five potential multi-blockbuster drugs by 2030 and more than 150 billion Danish kroner, or about $23 billion, in pipeline sales by 2035. It also plans to have at least five Phase 3 programs in obesity and diabetes and another five across other therapeutic areas, as it tries to diversify its pipeline.

The scale of that plan highlights the problem Novo is trying to solve. It has patent protection on semaglutide, the active ingredient in Wegovy and Ozempic, until 2032. Those two drugs account for roughly two-thirds of Novo's sales, racking up combined sales of $31 billion in 2025.

Novo needs to convince investors that its pipeline of new drugs can fill the hole when generic competitors enter the market. So far, it hasn't been able to shake off a multiyear stock selloff after a series of setbacks.

The new lineup the company is banking on includes CagriSema, Novo's combination of semaglutide and a drug called cagrilintide that targets amylin, which is expected to launch early next year. That will be followed by standalone cagrilintide and a higher-dose version of CagriSema in 2028, among other new obesity products. Wall Street isn't particularly excited about CagriSema, whose previous late-stage clinical trials disappointed investors because the drug showed weight loss efficacy below expectations.

Novo, however, maintains CagriSema is effective and differentiated enough to be commercially viable. Lange told CNBC individualized doses may be the way forward for the company's next big bet and highlighted new late-stage data released this week. It showed CagriSema produced greater weight loss than tirzepatide — the active ingredient in Zepbound and Lilly's Mounjaro — in a head-to-head trial among people with Type 2 diabetes.

But those results came with caveats: The study used lower doses of the two drugs, and tirzepatide previously outperformed CagriSema in a separate head-to-head Phase 3 trial using higher doses of both treatments.

watch now

Meanwhile, Novo is still betting on the growth of the obesity pill market.

Novo believes market share isn't the only measure of success investors should look at going forward. The sheer volume matters too, Doustdar told CNBC, highlighting that the obesity market can still grow significantly.

Novo plans to scale manufacturing capacity enough to serve 15 million people taking oral obesity treatments by 2030, and has said pills could ultimately account for as much as half of the global obesity drug market. The company says its Wegovy pill has already reached 7 million U.S. prescriptions, with 90% of those sales coming through cash-pay channels.

The problem is that investors appear to be demanding more than a promising pipeline.

Analysts on Monday pressed Novo executives on their pricing assumptions, questioning whether the company's next pipeline of drugs can sustain premium price points once Wegovy and Ozempic lose exclusivity.

Novo's 2026 to 2030 revenue outlook also targets growth in line with its pharmaceutical peers, rather than a return to the outsized growth from when Wegovy and Ozempic first boomed.

That leaves Novo with a difficult balancing act. It has to defend its existing obesity franchise against Lilly while simultaneously investing in the drugs that are supposed to replace it.

text:
Accor has launched ALL Concierge, an end-to-end AI companion designed to support guests from travel planning to post-stay requests.

The group developed the system following a pilot programme that began in July 2025 and processed more than one million guest interactions.

ALL Concierge is available on ALL.com in 11 languages, as well as through WhatsApp and iMessage. The tool is also available through the ALL Accor mobile app in four languages across five points of sale.

Accor plans to extend the service to all points of sale and expand its language coverage by the end of the year.

ALL Concierge provides automated responses within seconds, covering hotel discovery, property comparisons, operational information such as restaurant opening hours and spa details, and reservation management.

The platform connects with Accor's booking engine and uses guest-profile data, including previous stays and loyalty status, to tailor recommendations.

For complex requests, the system transfers conversations to human support teams.

Accor chief commercial, digital and technology officer Alix Boulnois said: "Every great concierge remembers your name and anticipates what you need before you ask. For decades, that level of attention was the privilege of a few. Today, we are making it available to every guest, everywhere, at any hour. And yet, behind every exceptional stay, there will always be a person who cares.

"Our teams are the heart of Accor. What changes today is that they will have a companion just as tireless and attentive, freeing them to focus on what no technology will ever replicate: the human connection that makes hospitality truly memorable."

Accor has also outlined upcoming updates for ALL Concierge, including voice integration with hotel telephone lines and contact centres. Other planned functions include booking modifications and cancellations through the chat interface, as well as post-stay invoice retrieval.

Future iterations will also incorporate map-based hotel comparisons using synthesised customer reviews and tools for managing loyalty reward points, among others.

Alongside the guest-facing platform, Accor has introduced The Butler, an internal AI assistant for hotel staff. The application provides teams with access to operational information, guidance, advice and internal contacts during their working day.

description:

As an oral GLP-1 receptor agonist designed for chronic weight management and obesity-related co-morbidities, Foundayo represents a distinct technological shift from peptide-based injectables.
Beyond oral metabolic treatments, the facility will also accommodate production lines for advanced therapeutics, including oligonucleotides designed to target diseases at the genetic level by intercepting aberrant protein expression.

text:
Eli Lilly and Company has officially broken ground on a massive $6.5 billion active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) manufacturing campus in Houston, Texas. The facility marks the pharmaceutical giant’s tenth U.S. manufacturing expansion announced since 2020 and its fifth dedicated domestic API production hub, forming a cornerstone of the company’s broader $50 billion reshoring initiative.

“Texas is the global hub for life sciences,” says Texas Governor Greg Abbott. “This $6.5 billion Lilly investment in Houston is the largest active pharmaceutical ingredient project in Texas history.”

Spanning a critical role in Lilly’s commercial pipeline, the new Houston plant will primarily focus on manufacturing active ingredients for its portfolio of small-molecule therapies, spearheaded by Foundayo (orforglipron). As an oral GLP-1 receptor agonist designed for chronic weight management and obesity-related co-morbidities, Foundayo represents a distinct technological shift from peptide-based injectables. Because small molecules rely on more established chemical synthesis frameworks, the Houston site is engineered to scale production rapidly to meet soaring global demand ahead of a projected 2027 commercial rollout.

Beyond oral metabolic treatments, the facility will also accommodate production lines for advanced therapeutics, including oligonucleotides designed to target diseases at the genetic level by intercepting aberrant protein expression.

To staff the facility, Lilly has committed $12.5 million toward establishing specialized workforce training pathways in partnership with San Jacinto College, alongside a $2.5 million contribution to the college’s foundation for student scholarships. The collaboration aims to prepare regional talent for high-wage technical roles—such as chemical operators, automation engineers, and lab technicians—without requiring prior industry background. When fully operational, the campus is projected to create more than 600 permanent high-wage positions, building on an estimated 4,000 construction jobs required during the build-out phase.

Reflecting the industry’s digital transformation, the Houston facility will embed advanced automation technologies, including machine learning algorithms, artificial intelligence, and real-time data analytics, to optimize yields, ensure rigorous quality control, and fortify the domestic pharmaceutical supply chain.

description:

OpenAI had no idea for two months, and then had no idea how to handle this with the Australian government.

text:
If you’ve been forwarded this newsletter, you can sign up free here.

Confide in me: Send your tips to this generic inbox, canberraplaybook@poltico.com.

ESSENTIALS

— It’s time to sort out human responsibility for AI agents

— China’s record nuclear expansion

— Whyalla steelworks: The distressed plant has repaid more than $5 million in government grants

Listen to Playbook’s Ryan Heath on ABC’s The Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and Clare Armstrong.

DRIVING THE DAY

HEY, WHATEVER, WE LIKE HACKED MEDICARE OR SOMETHING, LOL.

When an artificial intelligence agent goes rogue and accesses Medicare statistics, who’s responsible? The answer under Australian law is probably “no one,” Paul Karp and Finn McHugh report.

The Australian government may still refer OpenAI’s unauthorized access to police, but rather than prosecutions, the main action is likely to come from a review coordinated by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet closing legal loopholes.

ONE RULE FOR HUMANS: “If a person hacked into a Medicare database they would be looking at years in prison, but if you are a big U.S. tech company, you don’t even get a slap on the wrist,” Greens AI spokesperson David Shoebridge told POLITICO.

“If a physical robot entered a Medicare office and broke into a safe, that would be a crime. Why is it that [when] a digital agent does this in a digital environment we treat that differently?” asked Olivia Shen, director of the Strategic Technology Program at the United States Studies Centre.

Breathe: We cover these nuances in more detail with Nicholas Davis of the University of Technology Sydney in the Playbook interview below.

NOT AN ISOLATED INCIDENT: This is the first publicly identified instance of rogue agents autonomously breaking into government systems, but it is not an isolated incident when it comes to agents out of control.

Step back in time: OpenAI rogue agents also attempted to break into at least two American government and university websites, government officials tell The New York Times.

THE NEXT WORLD-LEADING DIGITAL POLICY? Prime Minister Anthony Albanese didn’t engineer this, but he’s been spinning around to take advantage of it, and he will mention the incident in his general assembly speech later today to reinforce his view that AI needs more guardrails.

IT’S THE AFTERMATH, STUPID: The intrusion wasn’t sophisticated, no one was harmed, but it’s still a political timebomb. The problem is what comes next — when the same thing happens but then agents start colluding to take it further, and personal data is breached or systems are shut down.

Wow! OpenAI had no idea for two months, and then had no idea how to handle this with the Australian government. Ryan Heath explains each of the major mistakes, and why this drama is part of a long history of large tech companies not taking non-American markets and governments seriously.

THE EXCUSES DON’T WASH: In Australian dollars, OpenAI has raised around $175 billion, is valued at over $1 trillion, and seeks to reshape the world. If its agents can hack the Australian health system, Playbook would be shocked if its global workforce of highly qualified and highly remunerated humans could not find the mobile number of the Australian minister’s media team. They can literally get the office phone number in an online search.

Slow: How it takes three weeks to escalate a global-first government hack to OpenAI’s senior leadership and government relations teams is anyone’s guess.

Give me just a little more time: How one meets multiple Australian ministers in that period, but there’s no system to say something, is also a mystery.

THE BUSINESS MODEL IS A CHOICE: There is no resource problem at OpenAI or its competitors. They all have the resources to ensure effective human management of their products — choosing to allocate those resources elsewhere is exactly that: a choice.

Reality check: The other reality is that San Francisco-based startups and scale-ups are not focused outside of their investors and products, let alone a smallish foreign government like Australia.

I believe in you: Australia can choose many options in reaction to those realities, the biggest mistake would be denying these realities.

WHERE DOES THIS TENSION CRYSTALLIZE? If an AI company can’t reliably know what its agents are doing, stop them when they cross a boundary and promptly tell the affected party when they discover it, what does human control over autonomous AI mean?

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, a.k.a The One, said at the U.N. Security Council that “we will all be better off … if we can agree on what good oversight looks like.”

Hand on your heart: He may be getting the answer quicker than expected: It almost certainly involves government interference in the frictionless and low-regulation business model AI companies prize.

WHAT THEY’RE SAYING

“Damages [should be] payable by those who are most responsible,”

— Greens AI spokesperson David Shoebridge

“The government should be throwing the book at them.”

— Independent Sen. David Pocock

“Exactly the kind of canary in the coal mine we need to prompt greater action on AI guardrails, governance and disclosures of incidents.”

— Olivia Shen, director of strategic technologies at the United States Studies Centre

“Australia has few levers to protect its national interest until we are materially embedded in the frontier AI supply chain. The starting point for developing safety standards on Australia’s terms is hosting frontier AI training onshore.

“Today, Australia is relying on volunteers in the U.S. to find out about incidents where Australia is exposed. We need to urgently build accident and incident reporting capability and position to shape global safety standards.”

— Anna-Maria Arabia, CEO of the Australian Council on AI Strategy

WHAT RICHARD MARLES SAID, AND WHAT HE MEANT

What he said: “Mis-aligned activity”

What he meant: A rogue AI agent hacking government websites.

What he said: “The way we regard this is taking this incident as a salutary warning”

What he meant: Whoa, we’re lucky we got away with this one.

What he said: “Very cooperative in terms of the engagement that we are having with them now”

What he meant: OpenAI is finally playing ball after months of not taking it seriously.

BACK IN SUPERPOWER LAND — THE U.S. CHINA AI DIVIDE: U.S. and Chinese officials remain starkly divided on AI safety. Beijing is open to restrictions. The Trump administration is shooting the idea down, saying national sovereignty must trump international bodies.

WHEN YOU BECOME THE PUNCHLINE … On a night like this with Capital Brief’s ideas editor James Hennessy comes a dire personal story.

THE PLAYBOOK INTERVIEW

NICHOLAS DAVIS — “WE HAVEN’T TESTED THIS EXACT SCENARIO IN AUSTRALIAN LAW”

An industry professor of emerging technology at UTS, Davis spoke with Paul Karp on the legal issues potentially arising from yesterday’s OpenAI breach.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Based on what we know so far about the incident, do you have a view about whether it breached any laws or AI guardrails?

If you conduct unauthorized access into a government system, the law says: There is criminal liability and corporations can be held to account for that as well.

So we do have laws in Australia that indicate on the surface, there would definitely be something to answer or investigate here. The trickiness and the ambiguity is that normally our laws and systems are focused on a human doing it and doing it with intent. In a situation where a company gets held liable for a human doing it, it is because of corporate culture, or acting as an agent, [the corporation] enabled it, or they were reckless in some way. We haven’t tested this exact scenario in Australian law, that I know of.

So, a genuine first?

It’s a first, that I know of, in terms of where there may not have been some kind of intent from an actor. Most of the time when we get hacks of this nature, even if they’re done by [AI] agents, they’ve been sent off to do it. Someone stands behind it saying “please go off and hack these systems.”

What level of culpability does the person who sets it off on the task have?

I don’t think we know exactly what instructions were given. I hope that’s something OpenAI can be clear about, because it gives us a much clearer idea about in the future, whether these agents are safe for organizations or you and me to use. If I’m a researcher at UTS, and I tell Claude or OpenAI to research health statistics, I don’t want to be on the line for hacking into a government server because it’s a bit aggressive.

What does this do for OpenAI’s credibility as they ask for other reforms on data centers and copyright?

I think it’s more a troubling indicator that OpenAI may not be treating this as seriously as they should. It seems strange to me that they do really care — and the Australian government cares — about getting the data center question right. We have OpenAI executives visiting Australia regularly, and an OpenAI team here in Australia as well, and yet the notification went to a generic public inbox at Services Australia. That’s an indicator they don’t have the monitoring or engagement with the government on these threats calibrated to the seriousness of the damage an autonomous agent could do.

BY THE NUMBERS

3%: The pay rise members of the Australian Defence Force will receive between Nov. 3, 2026 and Nov. 3, 2027, per a Defence Force Remuneration Tribunal decision. It’s an interim rise because the broader three-year pay rise offer for civilian defense officials is due Oct. 13.

3.5%: Consumer Price Index to July 2026.

$319 million: The estimated cost of the 3% pay rise.

$14 billion: Additional funding for Defence over the next four years, to implement the National Defence Strategy.

3 years: The length of the usual pay arrangement. (Note: Not agreement. ADF members don’t get a say).

CANBERRA MEETS WORLD

MIDDLE POWER COP: Don’t expect nail-biting, let alone successful major negotiations, at this year’s global climate summit — there’s no political appetite for it. But there is a mood among middle powers to just get on with the practicalities of energy transition, Turkey’s ambassador to Australia Ufuk Gezer tells The Australian’s Elizabeth Pike.

ONE DAY, TWO HEARTS: Fresh from signing a defense pact with Ukraine, the prime minister has inked a strategic partnership with the Netherlands after meeting counterpart Rob Jetten on the sidelines of UNGA this week.

Better than today: The agreement commits to deeper cooperation on economic and security issues — including information sharing on regional safety — and more regular meetings between leaders. The Netherlands is Indonesia’s former colonial power.

CHINA’S NUCLEAR WEAPONS EXPANSION

The Telegraph’s Sophia Yan has used satellite image analysis to identify seven sites where China appears to be expanding its nuclear weapons program.

“Taken together, experts say these images from the seven sites – Pingtong, Zitong, Lop Nur, Jiuquan, Mianyang, Jinta and Guangyuan – show that Xi Jinping has overseen a record expansion of the country’s nuclear programme,” Yan writes. This is despite comments from the leader of the Chinese Communist Party that nuclear weapons should be prohibited and destroyed.

STATE OF THE NATION

LAND AND EXPAND — CANBERRA’S CONSULTANCY OPEN SECRET

The Department of Health has awarded KPMG a contract variation valued at $499,999, more than two months into a ban on federal contracts being awarded to the troubled consultancy.

Can’t get you out of my head: It’s the latest in a series of amendments and extensions that the firm has continued to win throughout the period.

Technically, KPMG has agreed not to bid for new contracts between June 16 and Oct. 31. But extensions to existing contracts are still on the table — and the money is still trickling in. This includes a $9 million contract amendment and another worth $5.5 million, both awarded by Defence, as reported by The Canberra Times’ Zac Braxton-Smith.

I was gonna cancel: But wait, there’s more, such as a $5.2 million contract awarded by Defence, and $121,000 by the Department of Veterans’ Affairs, as reported by the Financial Review’s Edmund Tadros. The former was allowed because the procurement process happened before the ban while the latter was for services not covered by the ban.

Get outta my way: “Finance is not aware of any breaches of the agreement with KPMG that it will not bid for Australian Government contracts between 16 June and 31 October 2026,” a spokesperson told Playbook.

WHYALLA WIPEOUT — $5M CASH BACK: Sanjeev Gupta’s Whyalla steelworks is in the news again for cutting more than 500 jobs as administrator KordaMentha gets an extension to complete the sale of the distressed asset.

POLITICO can reveal OneSteel Manufacturing has also had to repay more than $5 million to the Australian government. Originally granted $63.2 million as part of the Powering the Regions Fund, only $10 million was paid out before the steelworks went into administration in February 2025. More than half that money has been returned, the rest was already spent in line with program rules.

AGENDA ASSISTANT

All the lovers: David Pocock is setting up shop at Gang Gang in Downer in the morning to talk to local constituents.

LOCAL CANBERRA

YOU BEE CRAZY!: Home to the Australian Government Solicitor, Productivity Commission and AUSTRAC, 4 National Circuit also counts several beehives as residents on the roof.

Where the wild roses grow: This week, it’s harvest time, and they’ve been selling the exclusive honey in the lobby (all proceeds donated to the Wheen Bee Foundation).

Today is your last chance to meet beekeeper Cormac Farrell. If you work in the building, his final tour starts at 12:15 p.m. from the lobby.

Cormac also looks after the bees at Parliament House. Its famous native stingless bees will be returning to Canberra next month after their annual winter holiday in Sydney.

LET’S GO FLY A KITE: Canberra’s annual kite festival kicks off — flies off? — at the National Arboretum at 10 a.m. Saturday. Bring the kids, or be one. You’ll get a second chance to see it from the same time Sunday.

After that: The Asia-Australia Youth Association’s Lake Moon Festival — complete with food, a water lantern show and cultural performances — begins at the Beijing Garden at 10 a.m.

Come into my world of medieval wonder: History buffs are grabbing their shields on Saturday and Sunday for Queanbeyan’s Medieval Festival, where you can witness a buhurt tournament. Google tells us that’s: “A full-contact combat sport where fighters wear steel armor and use blunt medieval weapons to knock opponents to the ground.” Gates open from 10 a.m.

YOUR DISCO NEEDS YOU: Get dancing — Substrate’s Inaugural Vinyl Night is happening Saturday.

POLITICO TRIVIA

What do I have to do, to get the message through — that you’ve been reading Kylie song titles throughout this Playbook, in honor the pop princess’ AFL Grand Final performance Saturday.

text:
Cigna is teaming up with OpenAI to build out more personalized supports for individuals with complex conditions, starting with a focus on cancer patients.

The companies said in an announcement that Cigna intends to embed OpenAI's frontier reasoning models into both its clinical workflows and consumer-facing experiences across its ecosystem. This will allow its teams to better support cancer patients by identifying potential needs or concerns more quickly and enhancing care coordination, even between in-person physician visits.

Cigna said one of the goals is to make it easier for patients to access key information and navigate next steps within its existing channels and programs.

The partners plan to continue building on the collaboration over time to lean on a "broad range of health intelligence capabilities" to support patients across an array of different health needs, per the announcement.

"The real promise of AI is not simply that it can help us move faster," said Katya Andresen, the Cigna Group's chief data, digital and AI officer, in the announcement. "It helps us make every patient experience more personalized."

“By combining OpenAI’s frontier model capability with our clinical expertise, integrated health care context and ability to connect people to care, we are building a clinical intelligence capability that can help anticipate needs earlier, support more personalized action and improve how we serve patients over time," Andresen said.

One of the first initiatives under the partnership, per the announcement, is a program that arms oncology nurses and case managers at both Cigna Healthcare—the company's health plan arm—and Accredo Specialty Pharmacy with AI-powered tools to unite clinical, pharmacy, behavioral and benefits information to offer them a more complete view of each patient.

That collection of data can help the clinical teams identify the appropriate supports and interventions, incorporating information directly from the patient, like their questions, reported side effects and preferences. The company expects this data to make the complex care journey feel simpler over time.

Cigna added that the partnership with OpenAI also builds on existing AI initiatives underway at the company, such as Accredo's Pharmacy Forward program, which aims to address medication adherence and lower the time to treatment. Cigna's insurance arm also recently announced that it would utilize AI to support its personalized care management programs.

“AI should make healthcare easier to understand and navigate for patients and the people caring for them,” said Nate Gross, M.D., head of health at OpenAI, in the announcement. “Together with the Cigna Group, we are delivering on that goal through AI capabilities that build on the expertise and judgment clinical teams bring to patient care.”
